videoIdeas.title: The 3 fears that make you a bad speaker
videoIdeas.hook: You're not bad at public speaking. You're just terrified of being seen.
videoIdeas.rationale: Public speaking is one of your three pillars and you have zero posts on it right now — that's a glaring gap. Whiteboard/explainer formats are crushing it for @saffanabanana (her media literacy video hit 29k), so a tight, named-list breakdown fits what's working in the niche.
videoIdeas.script: You're not bad at public speaking. You're just terrified of being seen. There are three fears doing all the damage, and none of them are about the words. One: you think everyone's watching you. They're not. They're thinking about themselves, same as you. Two: you think a shaky voice means you've failed. It doesn't. Nobody remembers the shake, they remember whether you had something to say. Three: you think you need to sound impressive. You don't. You need to be understood. Drop the fancy words. Say the true thing plainly. The best speakers in any room aren't the loudest. They're the ones who stopped performing and started talking.

visuals.setting: Plain wall or whiteboard, standing, shirt or smart casual. Calm, direct energy — eye contact with the lens, minimal hand movement, like you're correcting someone.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'You're not bad at speaking' while you hold up three fingers, then cut as you say the real line.
otherHookIdeas: Cold open mid-sentence: start on 'Two:' then jump-cut back to the top
Whiteboard with the 3 fears already written and crossed out
Pattern interrupt — start by deliberately stammering, then stop and say 'see, you already judged me'

videoIdeas.title: Leadership isn't the loudest person in the room
videoIdeas.hook: The loudest person in the room is almost never the leader. Here's who actually is.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your best-performing post ('I am in the room') proves your audience responds to quiet-confidence framing. Leadership is a core pillar but underfed. Named, counter-intuitive takes are doing numbers for @doctordaanish and @lifeofdinoo_.
videoIdeas.script: The loudest person in the room is almost never the leader. We've got it backwards. We think leadership is volume — talk the most, decide the fastest, never look unsure. It's the opposite. The real leader is the one everyone looks at before they answer a hard question. Not because he shouts, but because he's calm when it's bad. Anyone can lead when things are easy. You find out who the leader is the second it goes wrong. So stop trying to be heard. Start being the person people trust when it matters. That's the whole job.

visuals.setting: Walking shot outdoors or a quiet office/corridor. Movement adds authority. Darker, composed tone, not hyped.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open walking toward camera with on-screen text 'The loudest ≠ the leader'.
otherHookIdeas: Cut between a chaotic clip and a still shot of you to visualise noise vs calm
On-screen text punchline that lands on 'you find out when it goes wrong'
Start on a close-up, pull back to reveal you're the one everyone's facing

videoIdeas.title: History lesson: how Tariq bin Ziyad led men who wanted to quit
videoIdeas.hook: He burned the boats so his men couldn't run. Everyone quotes it. Almost nobody understands it.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your Andalusia/Tariq bin Ziyad post pulled 437 views with Islamic history framing — a lane your competitors largely ignore. Combining that proven subject with the leadership pillar plays to your strength and fills a gap.
videoIdeas.script: He burned the boats so his men couldn't run. Everyone quotes it. Almost nobody understands it. Tariq bin Ziyad crossed into Spain outnumbered, in foreign land, with men who were already looking over their shoulder. So he removed the exit. Not to be dramatic — to end the debate. When retreat is an option, half your mind is spent planning it. He forced every ounce of focus forward. Here's what that means for you: the goals you keep failing are the ones you left a back door on. The side project you 'might' do. The habit you'll keep 'if it works out.' Close the door. Tell people. Make quitting more expensive than finishing. That's not motivation. That's engineering.

visuals.setting: Dim, serious setting — plain dark background, or over a map/historical imagery b-roll. Low, deliberate delivery.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text 'He burned the boats' over a flame or map visual, then cut to your face.
otherHookIdeas: Open on historical map b-roll with no face for 2 seconds
Text-on-screen punchline: 'close the door' as a hard cut
Whisper-level delivery for the first line, then normal volume — audio pattern interrupt

videoIdeas.title: Why your runs, your reps, your deen all collapse at the same time
videoIdeas.hook: When one part of your life falls apart, check the others. They usually went first.
videoIdeas.rationale: Your running posts ('I am in the room', park at night) are your most engaging content, and your burnout app post shows your audience cares about discipline under pressure. @doctordaanish's journaling/habits videos hit 24k — habit/mindset content is hot. This merges your personal running angle with mindset.
videoIdeas.script: When one part of your life falls apart, check the others. They usually went first. You think you lost motivation to train. No — you stopped praying on time three weeks ago, your sleep went, then the gym went, then everything. It's never one thing. Discipline isn't a bunch of separate habits. It's one muscle wearing different clothes. The guy who shows up to Fajr is the same guy who shows up to the run he doesn't feel like doing. So when you're slipping, don't try to fix all five things. Fix the first domino — usually the small one you quietly dropped — and watch the rest come back. You don't need more willpower. You need to stop lying about where it broke.

visuals.setting: Film mid-run or right after one, slightly out of breath, outdoor, natural light. Raw and real — leans into your running brand.
visuals.visualHook: Cold open mid-run, breathing hard, on-screen text 'it was never the gym'.
otherHookIdeas: Sweaty post-run selfie-style talking to camera
On-screen domino graphic falling as you list the collapse
Start on the punchline 'stop lying about where it broke' then rewind

videoIdeas.title: Stop rehearsing in your head — rehearse out loud like an idiot
videoIdeas.hook: You've practised that speech a hundred times. In your head. That's why it falls apart out loud.
videoIdeas.rationale: Second public speaking idea to properly claim the empty pillar. Practical, specific, contrarian advice — the exact tone @birdtart01 used to go viral with 'cold emails are your best friend' and the networking questions video (978k views). Actionable how-to is the format winning right now.
videoIdeas.script: You've practised that speech a hundred times. In your head. That's why it falls apart out loud. Your brain is a liar — in there, every sentence is smooth, you never stumble, the jokes land. Then you open your mouth in front of actual humans and nothing matches. Because you never trained the actual skill: saying words with air, in order, out loud. Rehearse in the car. Rehearse to the mirror. Rehearse to one friend who'll be honest. Feel yourself stumble and fix it while it's cheap — not on stage where it costs you. Speaking is physical. You can't think your way to fluent. You have to sound stupid in private so you sound sharp in public.

visuals.setting: Car or mirror setting to literally demonstrate the advice. Casual, mid-action energy. Can film yourself actually practising.
visuals.visualHook: Open in the car talking to yourself, then turn to camera: 'yeah, this. do this.'
otherHookIdeas: Split screen: 'in your head' calm vs 'out loud' flustered
On-screen text 'your brain is lying to you' as cold open
Mid-action — catch yourself stumbling on purpose then fix it on camera

videoIdeas.title: You don't have an audience problem, you have a courage problem
videoIdeas.hook: 1,000 followers, 50 views. You think the algorithm hates you. It doesn't — you're just posting safe.
videoIdeas.rationale: Self-aware, slightly meta take that works for a smaller account and signals honesty. Your Majid Freeman post (289 likes) proves that when you post something with conviction and a clear stance, engagement spikes — this video names that lesson directly and is highly shareable among creators in your niche.
videoIdeas.script: 1,000 followers, 50 views. You think the algorithm hates you. It doesn't — you're just posting safe. Look at your own page honestly. The posts that did nothing were the ones you could've copied from anyone. The one time you said something you actually believed, something that could cost you — it moved. That's not a coincidence. People don't share 'correct.' They share 'finally someone said it.' Safe content is invisible content. If you're not a little nervous to post it, nobody's going to feel anything reading it. Stop asking what'll perform. Start asking what you're actually willing to stand behind.

visuals.setting: Sitting, close framing, direct and a little confrontational — talking to the viewer like you're calling them out kindly. Neutral indoor background.
visuals.visualHook: On-screen text '1,000 followers. 50 views.' on a black screen, then cut to your face.
otherHookIdeas: Show a mock analytics screen with flat numbers as cold open
On-screen punchline 'safe = invisible' on a hard cut
Start by pointing at the camera: 'this one's for you specifically'

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: This is your best post for a reason — 921 views, 118 likes, 11 comments, by far your strongest engagement. The caption 'Might not be the fastest in the room. But I am in the room' is your voice at its sharpest: short, punchy, a reframe that rewards re-reading. It pairs a personal, provable action (running) with a mindset line, which is exactly the blend your audience responds to.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: You left it as a one-off. This line is a content pillar waiting to happen — turn 'being in the room' into a recurring mindset series. Also add a soft CTA or question ('what room are you scared to waln into?') to convert those 118 likers into comments, since comments are what pushed this post's reach.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: The Tariq bin Ziyad / Andalusia angle is a genuine differentiator — none of your four competitors are doing Islamic history as leadership content, and it still pulled 437 views. The caption opens with a concrete, surprising historical hook ('In 711 AD...') which is a strong scroll-stopper.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Zero comments on 437 views means it informed but didn't provoke a response. History alone isn't enough — you have to land the 'so what does this mean for me today' before the video ends. Tie the lesson to a decision the viewer faces this week, and the caption got cut off ('wasn't built t') — front-load the payoff so it survives the truncation.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 376 views and a healthy 45 likes with almost no effort — 'Never running through a park at night ever again 😭' works because it's relatable, funny, and human. It shows your audience likes you, not just your lessons, and reinforces your running identity which is clearly your most magnetic theme.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: It's pure moment with no takeaway, so it caps out as entertainment. You don't need to sermonise every post, but this type of clip is the perfect trojan horse to slip in one sharp mindset line at the end — keep the humour, add a single blunt sentence so casual viewers remember you stand for something.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: You picked a real, widely-felt problem — burnout — and opened by naming the audience ('whether you're a medical student or not'), which is good targeting. The 🔥🧯 visual metaphor is a nice touch and on-brand for the topic.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: Only 209 views and 21 likes — your weakest of the five, because it reads as a promo for the Sabr app more than your own take. Your audience engages when you give them your opinion, not a product pitch. Lead with your own blunt view on burnout (e.g. 'burnout isn't working too hard, it's working with no meaning'), earn the attention first, then mention the app as a footnote.

postSuggestions.whatsWorking: 289 likes — your highest like count of any post, which proves the Majid Freeman point I keep making: when you take a clear moral stance with conviction, your audience rewards it hard. The hadith framing ('change it with his hand... tongue... heart') gives it authority and shareability, and it fits your young-Muslim niche perfectly.
postSuggestions.whatToImprove: 289 likes but only 1 comment — people agreed but weren't invited to act or discuss. A post like this should end with a concrete ask ('tag one person, share this, here's the link'). Also it's a Sidecar/carousel, not video — your reach is clearly in video right now, so test this exact message as a talking-to-camera reel to multiply the views those 289 likers represent.
